items.meaning: To spend quality time with someone to learn about their recent life events and experiences.
items.example: It's been ages, we really must catch up properly soon and hear all your news.
items.plain: It's been ages, we really must meet soon and hear all your news.
items.note: Used when you haven't seen someone in a while and want a substantial conversation, not just a quick chat.

items.meaning: A polite and indirect way to ask a question or make a request.
items.example: I was wondering if you'd be free for dinner next Friday?
items.plain: Are you free for dinner next Friday?
items.note: A very common, polite opening for invitations or requests, making them sound less demanding.

items.meaning: To make a tentative booking or arrangement, subject to confirmation.
items.example: I can pencil you in for Tuesday evening, but I'll confirm the exact time tomorrow.
items.plain: I can tentatively book you for Tuesday evening, but I'll confirm the exact time tomorrow.
items.note: Informal and flexible, suggesting the plan isn't fully fixed yet. Often used when scheduling.

items.meaning: To meet someone unexpectedly, often by chance.
items.example: I ran into an old friend at the supermarket yesterday, which was a pleasant surprise.
items.plain: I met an old friend unexpectedly at the supermarket yesterday, which was a pleasant surprise.
items.note: Implies a chance encounter, not a planned meeting. Can be positive or neutral.

items.meaning: An invitation to a guest to relax and feel comfortable, as if in their own house.
items.example: Come in, make yourself at home, I'll just put the kettle on.
items.plain: Come in, relax and feel comfortable, I'll just put the kettle on.
items.note: A standard, warm welcome from a host to a guest. Very common and friendly.

items.text: I'm afraid I can't make it
items.form: I'm afraid I can't make it
items.meaning: A polite way to decline an invitation or state unavailability.
items.example: I'm afraid I can't make it to the party on Saturday, I've already got plans.
items.plain: I can't come to the party on Saturday, I've already got plans.
items.note: A standard, polite refusal. The 'I'm afraid' softens the directness.

items.meaning: Used to check if a proposed plan or idea is acceptable to others.
items.example: We could meet for coffee around 10 AM, how does that sound?
items.plain: We could meet for coffee around 10 AM, is that okay with you?
items.note: A common way to invite feedback on a suggestion, making it collaborative.

items.meaning: To collaborate with others to solve a problem or come up with an idea.
items.example: Let's put our heads together and figure out a good date for the reunion.
items.plain: Let's work together and figure out a good date for the reunion.
items.note: Suggests a collaborative effort, often for planning or problem-solving. Informal and friendly.

items.meaning: To be busy and unavailable for other activities.
items.example: I'm tied up with work all next week, so I can't meet for lunch.
items.plain: I'm busy with work all next week, so I can't meet for lunch.
items.note: A common, slightly informal way to say you are busy or occupied. Can be used for work or personal commitments.

items.meaning: To decline an invitation but suggest doing it at a later, unspecified time.
items.example: I can't make it tonight, but could we take a rain check for next week?
items.plain: I can't make it tonight, but could we do it next week instead?
items.note: A polite way to postpone, implying genuine interest in rescheduling. Very common.

items.meaning: An expression of regret that a significant amount of time has passed since seeing someone.
items.example: It's been too long, we really need to get together soon!
items.plain: We haven't seen each other in a long time, we really need to get together soon!
items.note: A warm, slightly informal phrase used when greeting someone you haven't seen in a while.

items.text: what have you been up to
items.form: What have you been up to
items.meaning: A common question to ask someone about their recent activities and experiences.
items.example: Long time no see! What have you been up to lately?
items.plain: Long time no see! What have you been doing recently?
items.note: A standard, friendly opening for catching up with someone you haven't seen in a while.

items.text: I wouldn't miss it for the world
items.form: I wouldn't miss it for the world
items.meaning: An emphatic way to accept an invitation, showing great enthusiasm.
items.example: Your birthday party? I wouldn't miss it for the world!
items.plain: Your birthday party? I definitely want to be there!
items.note: Expresses strong eagerness and commitment to attend an event. Very enthusiastic.

items.meaning: An informal way to give permission or encourage someone to do something.
items.example: Feel free to bring a plus one if you like, the more the merrier!
items.plain: You can bring a plus one if you like, the more the merrier!
items.note: A polite and welcoming way to offer options or permission to a guest.

items.meaning: To visit someone informally and without a prior appointment.
items.example: I might drop by your place later if I finish work early.
items.plain: I might visit your place later if I finish work early.
items.note: Suggests a casual, unplanned visit. Often used for friends or close acquaintances.

items.meaning: To phone someone.
items.example: I'll give him a call tomorrow to confirm the details for dinner.
items.plain: I'll phone him tomorrow to confirm the details for dinner.
items.note: A common, natural way to say 'phone someone'. Can be used for any purpose.

items.meaning: A request for information or a decision from someone.
items.example: Let me know if you're free next Tuesday, and we can plan something.
items.plain: Tell me if you're free next Tuesday, and we can plan something.
items.note: A very common, informal way to ask for an update or confirmation.

items.meaning: To agree to participate in an activity or event.
items.example: A board game night? Count me in! I love those.
items.plain: A board game night? I'll join! I love those.
items.note: An enthusiastic and informal way to accept an invitation or offer to participate.

items.meaning: To anticipate something with pleasure.
items.example: I'm looking forward to catching up with everyone at the reunion.
items.plain: I'm excited to catch up with everyone at the reunion.
items.note: A standard, polite way to express anticipation for a future event or meeting.

items.text: it was lovely to see you
items.form: It was lovely to see you
items.meaning: A polite and warm closing remark after meeting someone.
items.example: It was lovely to see you both, thanks for a wonderful evening!
items.plain: It was nice to see you both, thanks for a wonderful evening!
items.note: A common, friendly farewell, often used after social gatherings. Can be 'nice' or 'great' too.

items.meaning: A polite and friendly way to express enjoyment of an activity and suggest repeating it.
items.example: That was a great dinner, we should do this again soon!
items.plain: That was a great dinner, let's meet up again soon!
items.note: A common, informal closing remark after a pleasant social event, implying future plans.

items.meaning: An offer to pay for the next round of drinks or meal.
items.example: You got this round, I'll get the next one.
items.plain: You paid for this round, I'll pay for the next one.
items.note: A common, informal gesture of reciprocity when socializing, especially at a bar or restaurant.

items.meaning: To make a quick, informal visit to someone's home.
items.example: Why don't you pop over for a coffee sometime next week?
items.plain: Why don't you come over for a coffee sometime next week?
items.note: Suggests a casual, brief visit. More informal than 'drop by'.

items.meaning: To state one's availability for a specific day or time.
items.example: I'm free on Wednesday evening if you want to grab a drink.
items.plain: I'm available on Wednesday evening if you want to grab a drink.
items.note: A direct and common way to communicate availability when making plans.

items.meaning: An enthusiastic agreement to proceed with a plan or idea.
items.example: You want to go hiking next month? Sounds great, let's make it happen!
items.plain: You want to go hiking next month? Sounds great, let's do it!
items.note: Expresses eagerness and commitment to turn a plan into reality. Informal and positive.

items.meaning: A polite and hesitant way to express doubt about one's ability to do something.
items.example: I'm not sure I can make it to the early morning yoga class.
items.plain: I don't think I can make it to the early morning yoga class.
items.note: A soft refusal or expression of uncertainty, less direct than 'I can't'.

items.meaning: To contact someone, usually by phone or message.
items.example: If you're in town next week, give me a shout and we can meet up.
items.plain: If you're in town next week, contact me and we can meet up.
items.note: An informal way to ask someone to get in touch. Common in British English.

items.meaning: A polite and enthusiastic way to accept an invitation.
items.example: Go for a walk in the park? I'd love to!
items.plain: Go for a walk in the park? Yes, I want to!
items.note: A very common and warm way to accept an invitation. Can be followed by 'but' for a polite refusal.

items.meaning: A casual question asking what someone is doing or planning.
items.example: Hey, what are you up to this weekend?
items.plain: Hey, what are your plans for this weekend?
items.note: A very common, informal greeting and way to initiate conversation about plans.

items.meaning: A polite way to say you need to consult your schedule before committing.
items.example: That sounds interesting, I'll check my diary and get back to you.
items.plain: That sounds interesting, I'll check my schedule and get back to you.
items.note: A standard, polite response when you need to confirm availability. Common in British English.

items.meaning: To have a prior engagement or plan.
items.example: I can't join you for dinner, I've got something on that evening.
items.plain: I can't join you for dinner, I have a prior engagement that evening.
items.note: A common, informal way to decline an invitation due to a previous commitment.

items.meaning: To briefly make contact with someone to discuss something or update each other.
items.example: Let's touch base next week to finalize the details for the trip.
items.plain: Let's talk briefly next week to finalize the details for the trip.
items.note: Often used in a professional context, but also common among friends for planning. Slightly formal.

items.text: I'm really sorry to miss out
items.form: I'm really sorry to miss out
items.meaning: An expression of regret at not being able to participate in an enjoyable event.
items.example: I'm really sorry to miss out on the concert, but I'm out of town.
items.plain: I'm very sad I can't go to the concert, but I'm out of town.
items.note: A polite and sincere way to express disappointment when declining an invitation.

items.meaning: A very polite and warm way to say 'you are welcome' or to invite someone.
items.example: Thank you for the invitation! You're most welcome to stay at our place.
items.plain: Thank you for the invitation! You are very welcome to stay at our place.
items.note: A formal and gracious way to extend an invitation or respond to thanks. More formal than 'you're welcome'.

items.meaning: To get something to eat, usually quickly and informally.
items.example: Are you free to grab a bite after work?
items.plain: Are you free to get something to eat after work?
items.note: A very common, informal way to suggest eating together. Can be a full meal or a snack.

items.meaning: To promise to provide updates as new information becomes available.
items.example: I'm still waiting for confirmation, but I'll keep you posted on the plans.
items.plain: I'm still waiting for confirmation, but I'll update you on the plans.
items.note: A common, informal way to assure someone they will receive updates. Useful for ongoing plans.

items.meaning: A polite and indirect way to make a suggestion or request.
items.example: It would be great if you could join us for the picnic on Sunday.
items.plain: It would be nice if you could join us for the picnic on Sunday.
items.note: A gentle way to express a desire for someone's presence or help, without being demanding.

items.meaning: To visit someone's house for a short, informal period.
items.example: I'll pop round later this evening to drop off the book.
items.plain: I'll visit your house later this evening to drop off the book.
items.note: Similar to 'pop over', common in British English for a quick, casual visit.

items.meaning: To be overwhelmed with a large amount of work or tasks.
items.example: I'm swamped with deadlines this week, so I can't make it to the pub.
items.plain: I have too many deadlines this week, so I can't make it to the pub.
items.note: An informal way to express being extremely busy, often implying stress. More intense than 'tied up'.

items.meaning: A suggestion to meet socially.
items.example: It's been a while, let's get together for a coffee soon.
items.plain: It's been a while, let's meet for a coffee soon.
items.note: A very common, informal way to propose a social meeting. Versatile.

items.meaning: A polite and indirect way to say 'no'.
items.example: Are you free for lunch tomorrow? I'm afraid not, I have a prior engagement.
items.plain: Are you free for lunch tomorrow? No, I have a prior engagement.
items.note: A standard, polite refusal. Softer than a direct 'no'.

items.meaning: An unexpected event or issue has occurred, preventing one from doing something.
items.example: I have to cancel our plans for tonight, something's come up at work.
items.plain: I have to cancel our plans for tonight, an unexpected issue has occurred at work.
items.note: A common, slightly vague way to explain a cancellation without going into detail. Polite.

items.meaning: A promise to contact someone again soon.
items.example: Thanks for the chat, I'll be in touch about those dates next week.
items.plain: Thanks for the chat, I'll contact you about those dates next week.
items.note: A standard, polite way to end a conversation, indicating future communication.

items.meaning: An offer to pay for something, usually a meal or drinks.
items.example: Don't worry about the bill, it's on me tonight.
items.plain: Don't worry about the bill, I'll pay for it tonight.
items.note: An informal and generous offer to treat someone. Common in social settings.

items.meaning: To express willingness or pleasure in doing something.
items.example: I'm happy to host the next book club meeting at my place.
items.plain: I'm willing to host the next book club meeting at my place.
items.note: A common and friendly way to offer help or accept a task.

items.meaning: To make a quick, informal visit to a place or person.
items.example: I'll swing by your office later to pick up those documents.
items.plain: I'll visit your office later to pick up those documents.
items.note: Similar to 'drop by' or 'pop over', but often implies a brief stop on the way to somewhere else.

items.meaning: A suggestion to meet and talk about recent events in each other's lives.
items.example: It's been ages, we should catch up over coffee soon.
items.plain: It's been ages, we should meet and talk over coffee soon.
items.note: A very common, friendly suggestion to reconnect with someone you haven't seen in a while.

items.text: I'm really looking forward to it
items.form: I'm really looking forward to it
items.meaning: An enthusiastic expression of anticipation for a future event.
items.example: Thanks for the invitation, I'm really looking forward to it!
items.plain: Thanks for the invitation, I'm very excited about it!
items.note: A common and warm way to accept an invitation and show genuine enthusiasm.

items.meaning: A polite offer to a guest to provide them with food, drink, or other items.
items.example: Please sit down, can I get you anything to drink?
items.plain: Please sit down, would you like anything to drink?
items.note: A standard, polite question from a host to a guest, showing hospitality.

items.meaning: A polite and appreciative closing remark after a social gathering.
items.example: Thank you so much for having us, it was a lovely evening.
items.plain: Thank you so much for having us, it was a very nice evening.
items.note: A common, polite way for a guest to thank their host at the end of an event.

items.meaning: A polite and understated way to express uncertainty or doubt.
items.example: I'm not entirely sure what my plans are for next weekend yet.
items.plain: I don't know exactly what my plans are for next weekend yet.
items.note: A common hedge, making a statement less definitive and more polite. Useful for declining indirectly.

items.meaning: To call someone on the telephone.
items.example: I'll give you a ring later to confirm the details.
items.plain: I'll call you later to confirm the details.
items.note: A common, informal way to say 'I'll call you'. More common in British English.

items.meaning: A common way to make a suggestion or propose an idea.
items.example: How about we meet for brunch on Sunday instead?
items.plain: What if we meet for brunch on Sunday instead?
items.note: A versatile and informal way to suggest an alternative or new plan.

items.text: I'm afraid I have to decline
items.form: I'm afraid I have to decline
items.meaning: A formal and polite way to refuse an invitation.
items.example: Thank you for the kind invitation, but I'm afraid I have to decline.
items.plain: Thank you for the kind invitation, but I must refuse.
items.note: A more formal and slightly more direct refusal than 'I can't make it'.

items.meaning: A polite and appreciative closing remark after a social interaction.
items.example: Thank you for your company, it's been a pleasure catching up.
items.plain: Thank you for your company, it was nice catching up.
items.note: A standard, polite farewell, often used in slightly more formal social contexts.

items.meaning: To state one's availability to do a specific activity.
items.example: I'm free to meet for coffee any time after 3 PM.
items.plain: I'm available to meet for coffee any time after 3 PM.
items.note: A direct way to communicate availability for a particular activity.

items.meaning: To send someone a short message, usually by email or text.
items.example: If you have any questions, just drop me a line.
items.plain: If you have any questions, just send me a message.
items.note: An informal way to ask someone to contact you, often in writing. Common in British English.

items.text: I'm not really up for it
items.form: I'm not really up for it
items.meaning: To not feel like doing something or lack enthusiasm for it.
items.example: A big party tonight? I'm not really up for it, I'm quite tired.
items.plain: A big party tonight? I don't feel like it, I'm quite tired.
items.note: An informal way to decline, indicating a lack of energy or desire. Can sound a bit dismissive if not softened.

items.meaning: A warm and enthusiastic invitation for someone to join or visit.
items.example: We're having a small gathering next Saturday, we'd love to have you!
items.plain: We're having a small gathering next Saturday, we really want you to come!
items.note: A very common, friendly way to extend an invitation, showing genuine desire for their presence.

items.meaning: An informal way to confirm attendance at an event.
items.example: Okay, 7 PM at the restaurant. I'll see you there!
items.plain: Okay, 7 PM at the restaurant. I'll meet you there!
items.note: A common, casual confirmation of plans, implying agreement on time and place.

items.meaning: An informal and enthusiastic way to confirm a social arrangement.
items.example: Dinner on Friday? Sounds good, it's a date!
items.plain: Dinner on Friday? Sounds good, we have a plan!
items.note: A playful and informal way to confirm plans, often used for one-on-one meetings.

items.meaning: To leave briefly for a short, informal errand or visit.
items.example: I'm just popping out to the shops, I'll be back in 20 minutes.
items.plain: I'm just going out to the shops briefly, I'll be back in 20 minutes.
items.note: A common, informal phrase to announce a short, temporary departure. British English.

items.meaning: To provide advance notice or a warning about something.
items.example: I'll give you a heads-up if the meeting time changes.
items.plain: I'll inform you in advance if the meeting time changes.
items.note: An informal way to promise to inform someone of future developments. Useful for planning.

items.meaning: To contribute money or effort to a shared expense or task.
items.example: For the group gift, I'm happy to chip in £20.
items.plain: For the group gift, I'm happy to contribute £20.
items.note: An informal and friendly offer to contribute to a shared cost or effort.

items.meaning: An expression indicating that a significant amount of time has passed since something happened.
items.example: It's been a while since we last saw each other, hasn't it?
items.plain: We haven't seen each other for a long time, have we?
items.note: A common, understated way to acknowledge a long gap between meetings. Neutral tone.

items.meaning: To state that one is busy or unable to meet.
items.example: Unfortunately, I'm not available on that particular day.
items.plain: Unfortunately, I'm busy on that particular day.
items.note: A direct but polite way to decline an invitation or state unavailability.

items.meaning: A suggestion to arrange a new time for a cancelled or postponed meeting.
items.example: I can't make it today, let's reschedule for next week.
items.plain: I can't make it today, let's arrange a new time for next week.
items.note: A common and practical suggestion when a plan needs to be changed.

items.text: I'm looking forward to seeing you
items.form: I'm looking forward to seeing you
items.meaning: An expression of pleasant anticipation for an upcoming meeting.
items.example: See you on Friday, I'm looking forward to seeing you!
items.plain: See you on Friday, I'm excited to see you!
items.note: A standard, warm closing remark when confirming plans to meet someone.

items.meaning: An expression of regret or disappointment about a situation.
items.example: It's a shame you can't make it, we'll miss you!
items.plain: It's disappointing you can't make it, we'll miss you!
items.note: A common, empathetic response to someone declining an invitation. Informal.

items.meaning: A direct and firm confirmation of attendance.
items.example: Don't worry, I'll be there for your presentation.
items.plain: Don't worry, I will attend your presentation.
items.note: A straightforward and reassuring way to confirm one's presence.

items.meaning: To make contact with someone to see how they are or to get an update.
items.example: Hi, I'm just checking in to see if you're still free for coffee tomorrow.
items.plain: Hi, I'm just contacting you to see if you're still free for coffee tomorrow.
items.note: A common, informal way to initiate contact, often to confirm plans or inquire about well-being.

items.meaning: An offer to assist someone with a task or problem.
items.example: If you need an extra pair of hands for the party setup, I'm happy to help.
items.plain: If you need an extra pair of hands for the party setup, I'm willing to help.
items.note: A standard, friendly offer of assistance. Very common and polite.

items.meaning: A suggestion to maintain communication with someone.
items.example: It was great seeing you, let's keep in touch!
items.plain: It was great seeing you, let's stay in contact!
items.note: A common, friendly farewell, especially when you don't have immediate plans to meet again.

items.meaning: A promise to contact someone very soon.
items.example: I'm just finishing up here, I'll be in touch shortly to confirm.
items.plain: I'm just finishing up here, I'll contact you very soon to confirm.
items.note: A polite and professional way to indicate imminent communication. Slightly more formal than 'I'll be in touch'.

items.text: it's a pleasure to meet you
items.form: It's a pleasure to meet you
items.meaning: A polite and formal greeting when introduced to someone for the first time.
items.example: Hello, it's a pleasure to meet you, I've heard a lot about you.
items.plain: Hello, it's nice to meet you, I've heard a lot about you.
items.note: A standard, polite greeting. Can be shortened to 'Nice to meet you' for informality.

items.meaning: To be on the verge of doing something.
items.example: I'm just about to head out, but I can spare a minute.
items.plain: I'm going to leave very soon, but I can spare a minute.
items.note: Indicates immediate future action. Useful for managing expectations when someone calls or arrives.

items.meaning: A promise or commitment to do something.
items.example: I'll make sure to bring the dessert for the potluck.
items.plain: I promise to bring the dessert for the potluck.
items.note: A common way to confirm responsibility and assure someone that a task will be done.

items.text: I'm looking forward to hearing from you
items.form: I'm looking forward to hearing from you
items.meaning: A polite closing remark expressing anticipation for a response.
items.example: Let me know your availability, I'm looking forward to hearing from you.
items.plain: Let me know your availability, I'm excited to hear from you.
items.note: A standard, polite closing in communication, especially when awaiting a reply or decision.

items.meaning: An expression of genuine enjoyment and appreciation for an experience.
items.example: Thank you for the wonderful dinner, it's been a real treat.
items.plain: Thank you for the wonderful dinner, it was a truly enjoyable experience.
items.note: A warm and sincere way to express gratitude for a particularly pleasant social occasion.

items.text: I'm happy to go with the flow
items.form: I'm happy to go with the flow
items.meaning: To be flexible and adapt to whatever plans or decisions others make.
items.example: I don't have a strong preference, I'm happy to go with the flow.
items.plain: I don't have a strong preference, I'm happy to adapt to whatever you decide.
items.note: An informal way to express flexibility and willingness to adapt to group plans.

items.meaning: A promise to contact someone in the near future.
items.example: I'll confirm the details by email, I'll be in touch soon.
items.plain: I'll confirm the details by email, I'll contact you soon.
items.note: A common, polite way to end a conversation, indicating future communication. Less immediate than 'shortly'.

items.meaning: A common opening for a phone call, stating its purpose.
items.example: Hi Sarah, I'm just calling to see if you're free for coffee tomorrow.
items.plain: Hi Sarah, I'm calling to see if you're free for coffee tomorrow.
items.note: A standard, polite way to begin a phone conversation by explaining the reason for the call.

items.text: I'm not sure I can commit
items.form: I'm not sure I can commit
items.meaning: A polite and hesitant way to express uncertainty about being able to promise participation.
items.example: I'm not sure I can commit to the weekly study group right now.
items.plain: I don't know if I can promise to join the weekly study group right now.
items.note: A diplomatic way to decline or delay a commitment, often due to other obligations or uncertainty.

items.meaning: An expression used when encountering an unexpected connection or coincidence.
items.example: You know my cousin? Wow, it's a small world!
items.plain: You know my cousin? Wow, what a coincidence!
items.note: A common, informal phrase used to express surprise at an unexpected connection between people or places.

items.meaning: To make a quick, informal visit to a place or person.
items.example: I'm just popping in to say hello before I head home.
items.plain: I'm just visiting briefly to say hello before I head home.
items.note: Similar to 'popping out', but for arriving. Implies a brief, casual visit.

items.meaning: A promise to respond to someone at a later time.
items.example: I need to check my schedule, I'll get back to you about the dinner.
items.plain: I need to check my schedule, I'll respond to you about the dinner.
items.note: A common, polite way to say you will reply after checking information or making a decision.

items.meaning: To be pleased to help or do what someone has asked.
items.example: If you need me to pick up some groceries, I'm happy to oblige.
items.plain: If you need me to pick up some groceries, I'm pleased to help.
items.note: A polite and slightly formal way to express willingness to help or fulfill a request.

items.text: it's been a pleasure meeting you
items.form: It's been a pleasure meeting you
items.meaning: A polite closing remark after being introduced to someone for the first time.
items.example: Well, it's been a pleasure meeting you, I hope our paths cross again.
items.plain: Well, it was nice meeting you, I hope our paths cross again.
items.note: A standard, polite farewell after a first introduction. Slightly more formal than 'nice meeting you'.

items.meaning: A common opening for a phone call, stating its purpose.
items.example: Hi Mum, I'm just calling to say I'll be home a bit late.
items.plain: Hi Mum, I'm calling to tell you I'll be home a bit late.
items.note: A standard, informal way to begin a phone call by immediately stating the main message.

items.text: I'm not sure what my plans are
items.form: I'm not sure what my plans are
items.meaning: To express uncertainty about one's future activities.
items.example: I'm not sure what my plans are for the weekend, I'll let you know.
items.plain: I don't know what my plans are for the weekend, I'll let you know.
items.note: A common, informal way to indicate that one's schedule is not yet fixed. Can be a soft refusal.

items.text: I'll be there with bells on
items.form: I'll be there with bells on
items.meaning: An enthusiastic and informal way to confirm attendance, implying eagerness.
items.example: Your party? Absolutely, I'll be there with bells on!
items.plain: Your party? Absolutely, I'll be there and very excited!
items.note: A very informal and enthusiastic way to accept an invitation. Shows great eagerness.

items.meaning: To leave briefly to get or do something specific.
items.example: I'm just popping out for some milk, I'll be right back.
items.plain: I'm just going out briefly to get some milk, I'll be right back.
items.note: A common, informal phrase to explain a short, temporary departure for a specific purpose.

items.text: I'll keep an eye out for you
items.form: I'll keep an eye out for you
items.meaning: A promise to look for someone at a specific location or event.
items.example: It'll be busy at the concert, but I'll keep an eye out for you.
items.plain: It'll be busy at the concert, but I'll look for you.
items.note: A common, informal way to assure someone you'll try to find them in a crowd.

items.meaning: To contribute effort or help with a task, often as part of a group.
items.example: If you need help setting up for the party, I'm happy to pitch in.
items.plain: If you need help setting up for the party, I'm happy to help.
items.note: Similar to 'chip in', but often implies contributing effort rather than just money. Informal.

items.meaning: An expression indicating that a significant period has passed since something occurred.
items.example: It's been a long time since we last had a proper chat.
items.plain: We haven't had a proper chat for a long time.
items.note: A common, neutral way to acknowledge a long interval. Similar to 'it's been a while'.

items.meaning: A common opening for a phone call, stating the topic of discussion.
items.example: Hi, I'm just calling about the dinner plans for Saturday.
items.plain: Hi, I'm calling about the dinner plans for Saturday.
items.note: A standard, polite way to begin a phone conversation by immediately stating the subject.

items.meaning: A strong promise or commitment to do something.
items.example: I'll be sure to send you the photos from the party.
items.plain: I promise to send you the photos from the party.
items.note: A common way to emphasize certainty and commitment to an action.

items.meaning: To make a quick, informal visit to a place or person.
items.example: I'm just popping by to drop off this book you lent me.
items.plain: I'm just visiting briefly to drop off this book you lent me.
items.note: Similar to 'popping in', but often implies a very brief stop, perhaps without staying long.

items.text: I'll be in touch with you
items.form: I'll be in touch with you
items.meaning: A promise to contact someone.
items.example: I'll check my schedule and I'll be in touch with you about next week.
items.plain: I'll check my schedule and I'll contact you about next week.
items.note: A standard, polite way to indicate future communication. Slightly more formal than 'I'll be in touch'.

items.meaning: To express willingness to give money, time, or effort to a shared cause.
items.example: For the charity event, I'm happy to contribute some baked goods.
items.plain: For the charity event, I'm willing to give some baked goods.
items.note: A polite and common way to offer help or resources. Can be for money, items, or effort.

items.text: it's been a pleasure working with you
items.form: It's been a pleasure working with you
items.meaning: A polite and appreciative closing remark in a professional or collaborative context.
items.example: As I'm leaving the company, it's been a pleasure working with you all.
items.plain: As I'm leaving the company, it was nice working with you all.
items.note: A standard, polite farewell in a work or project setting. Can be adapted for social projects.

items.meaning: A common opening for a phone call, stating the purpose of verifying information.
items.example: Hi, I'm just calling to confirm our meeting for tomorrow morning.
items.plain: Hi, I'm calling to confirm our meeting for tomorrow morning.
items.note: A standard, polite way to begin a phone call by stating the intention to verify details.

items.meaning: A promise to contact someone at a subsequent, unspecified time.
items.example: I'm busy right now, but I'll be in touch later today.
items.plain: I'm busy right now, but I'll contact you later today.
items.note: A common, informal way to indicate future communication, but not immediately.

items.meaning: An offer to assist with a task or situation, often implying a small contribution.
items.example: If you need an extra hand with the decorations, I'm happy to help out.
items.plain: If you need an extra hand with the decorations, I'm willing to assist.
items.note: A common, informal offer of assistance, often for a specific task or event.

items.text: it's been a pleasure having you
items.form: It's been a pleasure having you
items.meaning: A polite and warm closing remark from a host to a guest.
items.example: Thank you for visiting, it's been a pleasure having you stay with us.
items.plain: Thank you for visiting, it was nice having you stay with us.
items.note: A standard, polite farewell from a host, expressing enjoyment of the guest's company.

items.meaning: A common opening for a phone call, stating the purpose of making an inquiry.
items.example: Hi, I'm just calling to ask if you're free for dinner next week.
items.plain: Hi, I'm calling to ask if you're free for dinner next week.
items.note: A standard, polite way to begin a phone call by immediately stating the intention to ask a question.

items.text: I'll be in touch as soon as
items.form: I'll be in touch as soon as
items.meaning: A promise to contact someone immediately after a specific event or condition is met.
items.example: I'll be in touch as soon as I have the final details.
items.plain: I'll contact you immediately after I have the final details.
items.note: A common way to promise prompt communication once certain information is available.

items.meaning: To express willingness to adjust one's schedule to accommodate something.
items.example: Even though I'm busy, I'm happy to make time for your birthday celebration.
items.plain: Even though I'm busy, I'm willing to find time for your birthday celebration.
items.note: A polite and accommodating way to show willingness to meet despite a busy schedule.

items.text: it's been a pleasure getting to know you
items.form: It's been a pleasure getting to know you
items.meaning: A polite closing remark after developing a new acquaintance.
items.example: After our project, it's been a pleasure getting to know you better.
items.plain: After our project, it was nice getting to know you better.
items.note: A warm and polite farewell, often used after spending some time with a new acquaintance.

items.text: I'm just calling to follow up
items.form: I'm just calling to follow up
items.meaning: A common opening for a phone call, stating the purpose of checking on a previous matter.
items.example: Hi, I'm just calling to follow up on our conversation about the weekend trip.
items.plain: Hi, I'm calling to check on our conversation about the weekend trip.
items.note: A standard, polite way to begin a phone call by referring to a previous discussion or action.

items.text: I'll be in touch by the end of
items.form: I'll be in touch by the end of
items.meaning: A promise to contact someone before a specific deadline.
items.example: I'll be in touch by the end of the week with the updated schedule.
items.plain: I'll contact you before the end of the week with the updated schedule.
items.note: A common way to set a clear expectation for when communication will occur.

items.text: I'm happy to lend a hand
items.form: I'm happy to lend a hand
items.meaning: An offer to help someone with a task or problem.
items.example: If you need help moving furniture, I'm happy to lend a hand.
items.plain: If you need help moving furniture, I'm willing to help.
items.note: A common, informal offer of assistance. Very friendly and helpful.

items.text: it's been a pleasure meeting all of you
items.form: It's been a pleasure meeting all of you
items.meaning: A polite closing remark when introduced to a group of people for the first time.
items.example: Thank you for the lovely evening, it's been a pleasure meeting all of you.
items.plain: Thank you for the lovely evening, it was nice meeting all of you.
items.note: A standard, polite farewell when leaving a group after initial introductions.

items.text: I'm just calling to let you know
items.form: I'm just calling to let you know
items.meaning: A common opening for a phone call, stating the purpose of conveying information.
items.example: Hi, I'm just calling to let you know I'll be a few minutes late.
items.plain: Hi, I'm calling to tell you I'll be a few minutes late.
items.note: A standard, polite way to begin a phone call by immediately sharing important information.

items.meaning: A promise to contact someone about a specific topic.
items.example: I'll be in touch regarding the details for the upcoming event.
items.plain: I'll contact you about the details for the upcoming event.
items.note: A slightly more formal way to promise communication about a particular subject.

items.meaning: To express willingness to participate in an activity.
items.example: If you're playing board games, I'm happy to join in!
items.plain: If you're playing board games, I'm willing to participate!
items.note: A common, informal way to express enthusiasm for joining an activity.

items.text: it's been a pleasure having you over
items.form: It's been a pleasure having you over
items.meaning: A polite and warm closing remark from a host to a guest who has visited their home.
items.example: Thank you for coming, it's been a pleasure having you over.
items.plain: Thank you for coming, it was nice having you visit our home.
items.note: A standard, polite farewell from a host after guests have visited their home.

items.text: I'm just calling to catch up
items.form: I'm just calling to catch up
items.meaning: A common opening for a phone call, stating the purpose of reconnecting and sharing news.
items.example: Hi, I'm just calling to catch up and see how you're doing.
items.plain: Hi, I'm calling to reconnect and see how you're doing.
items.note: A standard, informal way to begin a phone call with a friend to share updates.

items.text: I'll be in touch with an update
items.form: I'll be in touch with an update
items.meaning: A promise to contact someone to provide new information.
items.example: I'll check the schedule and I'll be in touch with an update.
items.plain: I'll check the schedule and I'll contact you with new information.
items.note: A common, polite way to promise to provide further details or progress reports.

items.text: I'm happy to help out where I can
items.form: I'm happy to help out where I can
items.meaning: An offer to assist as much as possible, acknowledging potential limitations.
items.example: I can't commit to everything, but I'm happy to help out where I can.
items.plain: I can't commit to everything, but I'm willing to help as much as possible.
items.note: A polite and flexible offer of assistance, often used when one cannot fully commit.

items.text: it's been a pleasure spending time with you
items.form: It's been a pleasure spending time with you
items.meaning: A polite and warm closing remark after a period of social interaction.
items.example: Thank you for the weekend, it's been a pleasure spending time with you.
items.plain: Thank you for the weekend, it was nice spending time with you.
items.note: A standard, polite farewell after a social occasion, expressing enjoyment of company.

items.meaning: A common opening for a phone call, stating the purpose of making plans.
items.example: Hi, I'm just calling to arrange a time for us to meet next week.
items.plain: Hi, I'm calling to plan a time for us to meet next week.
items.note: A standard, polite way to begin a phone call by stating the intention to schedule something.

items.meaning: A polite way to ask about someone's availability for a meeting or activity.
items.example: Would you be free for a quick coffee sometime next week?
items.plain: Are you available for a quick coffee next week?
items.note: A common, polite way to initiate plans. More open-ended than asking about a specific day.

items.meaning: Asks for someone's opinion or reaction to a suggestion or idea.
items.example: I was thinking of a picnic in the park; how does that strike you?
items.plain: I was thinking of a picnic in the park; what do you think?
items.note: A slightly more formal or thoughtful way to ask for feedback on a proposal.

items.meaning: Expresses a desire or intention, often as a gentle suggestion for plans.
items.example: I was hoping to get everyone together for a board game night soon.
items.plain: I want to get everyone together for a board game night soon.
items.note: A soft, indirect way to propose an activity, making it less demanding.

items.meaning: Suggests scheduling a specific time for an event or meeting.
items.example: We should really put a date in the diary for that dinner we discussed.
items.plain: We should schedule that dinner we discussed.
items.note: Common in British English, often followed by 'the diary' or 'the calendar'.

items.meaning: Asks for someone's opinion or perspective on a particular idea or plan.
items.example: What's your take on meeting up for brunch this Sunday?
items.plain: What do you think about meeting up for brunch this Sunday?
items.note: A casual yet sophisticated way to solicit an opinion or preference.

items.meaning: Asks if someone would like to do something or is interested in an activity.
items.example: Do you fancy grabbing a drink after work on Friday?
items.plain: Would you like to grab a drink after work on Friday?
items.note: Common in British English, less so in American English. Casual and friendly.

items.meaning: Expresses a strong desire to organize or set up a meeting or event.
items.example: I'm keen to arrange a proper catch-up with you soon.
items.plain: I really want to organize a proper catch-up with you soon.
items.note: Indicates enthusiasm and initiative. 'Keen' is more common in British English.

items.meaning: Emphasizes a strong suggestion or intention to do something together.
items.example: We should definitely try that new restaurant everyone's talking about.
items.plain: Let's try that new restaurant everyone's talking about.
items.note: A friendly and enthusiastic way to propose an activity.

items.meaning: Indicates an intention to organize and host a social event.
items.example: I'm thinking of hosting a small gathering at my place next month.
items.plain: I might host a small gathering at my place next month.
items.note: A casual way to float an idea for an event without a firm commitment yet.

items.meaning: Asks if someone is receptive to a particular idea or activity.
items.example: Are you open to joining us for a hike this weekend?
items.plain: Would you like to join us for a hike this weekend?
items.note: A polite and inclusive way to invite someone, suggesting flexibility.

items.meaning: Suggests finding a mutually convenient time for multiple people.
items.example: It's tricky with everyone's commitments, so let's coordinate our schedules.
items.plain: It's hard with everyone's commitments, so let's find a time that works.
items.note: A practical and slightly formal way to suggest finding a shared availability.

items.text: I'd be delighted to have you
items.form: I'd be delighted to have you
items.meaning: A very polite and warm way to invite someone to your home or event.
items.example: I'd be delighted to have you over for dinner next Saturday.
items.plain: I would love for you to come over for dinner next Saturday.
items.note: A gracious and welcoming invitation, often used for more formal or special occasions.

items.meaning: A direct and clear way to extend an invitation to someone.
items.example: Consider this an invitation to our annual summer barbecue.
items.plain: You are invited to our annual summer barbecue.
items.note: A slightly formal but friendly way to ensure someone knows they are invited.

items.meaning: Asks about someone's free time or schedule for making plans.
items.example: What's your availability like for a call next week?
items.plain: When are you free for a call next week?
items.note: A professional yet friendly way to inquire about someone's schedule.

items.meaning: Suggests making a special effort to find time for something despite a busy schedule.
items.example: We're both so busy, but let's try and carve out some time to meet.
items.plain: We're both so busy, but let's try to find some time to meet.
items.note: Implies that time is scarce and requires effort to find, often used with 'time'.

items.meaning: Expresses a strong interest or desire to do something.
items.example: I'm quite keen to hear all about your recent travels.
items.plain: I really want to hear all about your recent travels.
items.note: A polite and enthusiastic way to show interest. 'Quite' softens it slightly.

items.meaning: A very polite and somewhat formal way to invite someone to an activity.
items.example: Would you care to join us for a concert next month?
items.plain: Would you like to join us for a concert next month?
items.note: More formal than 'Do you fancy' or 'Would you like to'. Elegant and refined.

items.meaning: Indicates willingness to adjust one's schedule to accommodate another's.
items.example: I'm flexible around your work schedule, just let me know what works.
items.plain: I can adjust to your work schedule, just tell me what works.
items.note: A helpful and accommodating phrase when making plans.

items.meaning: Asks for someone's preferred time for a meeting or activity.
items.example: What time suits you best for our meeting on Tuesday?
items.plain: What time is most convenient for you for our meeting on Tuesday?
items.note: A standard, polite way to inquire about preferred timing.

items.meaning: Indicates willingness to consider other ideas or options for a plan.
items.example: I'm open to suggestions for a good place to eat downtown.
items.plain: I'll consider any ideas for a good place to eat downtown.
items.note: Shows flexibility and encourages input from others when making plans.

items.meaning: Expresses a desire for a plan to materialize, often after previous attempts.
items.example: I'm hoping we can make that coffee date happen soon.
items.plain: I hope we can have that coffee date soon.
items.note: Conveys a gentle push to finalize plans, implying it's been pending.

items.meaning: Expresses enthusiastic willingness to participate if the other person is also willing.
items.example: I'm game if you are for a spontaneous road trip this weekend.
items.plain: I'm willing to go if you are for a spontaneous road trip this weekend.
items.note: A casual and enthusiastic way to agree to a plan, often spontaneous ones.

items.meaning: Expresses strong agreement or support for a suggestion or idea.
items.example: A quiet evening in sounds perfect, I'm all for that.
items.plain: A quiet evening in sounds perfect, I completely agree.
items.note: A warm and enthusiastic way to show approval for a plan.

items.meaning: Expresses a moderate to strong feeling of anticipation and pleasure.
items.example: I'm quite excited about the prospect of seeing everyone again.
items.plain: I'm looking forward to seeing everyone again.
items.note: A polite and genuine way to convey enthusiasm without being overly effusive.

items.meaning: Expresses great pleasure and enthusiasm about an invitation or opportunity.
items.example: I'd be thrilled to join you for the celebration.
items.plain: I would be very happy to join you for the celebration.
items.note: A strong and genuine expression of happiness to accept an invitation.

items.meaning: A formal and very polite way to agree to an invitation.
items.example: I'm delighted to accept your kind invitation to the party.
items.plain: I'm very happy to accept your invitation to the party.
items.note: A gracious and appreciative way to formally accept an invitation.

items.meaning: Expresses a feeling of privilege or special recognition for being invited.
items.example: I'm honoured to be invited to such a special event.
items.plain: I feel privileged to be invited to such a special event.
items.note: Used for significant or exclusive invitations, conveying deep appreciation.

items.meaning: A formal way to state that one will attend an event.
items.example: I'm pleased to confirm my attendance at your gathering.
items.plain: I'm happy to say I will be at your gathering.
items.note: Often used in written communication or for more formal events.

items.meaning: A firm and reassuring commitment to attend an event.
items.example: I'll certainly be there, looking forward to catching up.
items.plain: I will definitely be there, looking forward to catching up.
items.note: Conveys strong intention and reliability, often used with enthusiasm.

items.meaning: A strong assurance that one will be able to attend an event.
items.example: I'll definitely make it to your housewarming party.
items.plain: I will certainly be able to come to your housewarming party.
items.note: A common and confident way to confirm attendance.

items.text: I'll be sure to come along
items.form: I'll be sure to come along
items.meaning: A polite and friendly way to confirm attendance at an event.
items.example: I'll be sure to come along, thanks for thinking of me.
items.plain: I will definitely come, thanks for thinking of me.
items.note: Conveys a positive and reliable intention to join.

items.text: I wouldn't miss it for anything
items.form: I wouldn't miss it for anything
items.meaning: Expresses extreme eagerness and determination to attend an event.
items.example: Your birthday bash? I wouldn't miss it for anything!
items.plain: Your birthday party? I absolutely must be there!
items.note: A very enthusiastic and emphatic way to accept an invitation.

items.meaning: Expresses warm approval and pleasure regarding a suggestion or plan.
items.example: A quiet dinner at your place? That sounds absolutely lovely.
items.plain: A quiet dinner at your place? That sounds wonderful.
items.note: A very positive and appreciative response, common in British English.

items.meaning: Expresses strong and excited expectation for a future event.
items.example: I'm eagerly anticipating our long-overdue catch-up.
items.plain: I'm really looking forward to our long-overdue catch-up.
items.note: A more sophisticated and slightly formal way to express excitement.

items.meaning: Expresses willingness and pleasure to participate in an activity.
items.example: I'm happy to join you for the concert if there are tickets left.
items.plain: I'd be pleased to join you for the concert if there are tickets left.
items.note: A straightforward and friendly way to accept an invitation.

items.meaning: Confirms that one can attend an event, often after previous uncertainty.
items.example: Good news, I'm able to make it after all, so count me in!
items.plain: Good news, I can come after all, so include me!
items.note: Often used when confirming availability after checking one's schedule.

items.meaning: A polite and enthusiastic way to accept an invitation.
items.example: I'll be there with pleasure, thank you for the invitation.
items.plain: I will gladly be there, thank you for the invitation.
items.note: Conveys both acceptance and appreciation for the invitation.

items.text: I'm looking forward to it immensely
items.form: I'm looking forward to it immensely
items.meaning: Expresses a very strong degree of anticipation and excitement.
items.example: I'm looking forward to it immensely, it sounds like a wonderful evening.
items.plain: I'm really looking forward to it, it sounds like a wonderful evening.
items.note: A more emphatic and sophisticated way to express excitement than 'very much'.

items.meaning: A very polite and apologetic way to decline an invitation or deliver bad news.
items.example: I'm terribly sorry but I already have a prior engagement.
items.plain: I'm very sorry but I already have another plan.
items.note: A sincere and empathetic way to express regret when declining.

items.text: I'm afraid I have other commitments
items.form: I'm afraid I have other commitments
items.meaning: A polite way to decline an invitation by stating existing obligations.
items.example: I'm afraid I have other commitments that evening, so I can't join.
items.plain: Unfortunately, I have other plans that evening, so I can't join.
items.note: A common and diplomatic way to decline without giving too much detail.

items.meaning: Explains that one has two conflicting appointments or plans at the same time.
items.example: I'm afraid I'm double-booked for that specific time slot.
items.plain: Unfortunately, I have two things scheduled for that specific time.
items.note: A common and clear reason for declining, implying it's an unavoidable conflict.

items.text: Regrettably, I won't be able to
items.form: Regrettably, I won't be able to
items.meaning: A formal and apologetic way to state inability to attend or participate.
items.example: Regrettably, I won't be able to attend your event.
items.plain: Unfortunately, I won't be able to attend your event.
items.note: A more formal and slightly understated way to decline, conveying sincere regret.

items.meaning: A polite and understated way to say one is feeling unwell or not in good spirits.
items.example: I'm not feeling entirely myself today, so I think I'll stay in.
items.plain: I'm not feeling very well today, so I think I'll stay in.
items.note: A subtle way to indicate mild illness or low energy without oversharing.

items.text: I'm afraid I'm not up to
items.form: I'm afraid I'm not up to
items.meaning: Politely states that one lacks the energy or inclination for an activity.
items.example: I'm afraid I'm not up to a big social gathering tonight.
items.plain: Unfortunately, I don't have the energy for a big social gathering tonight.
items.note: A gentle way to decline, implying a lack of energy or mood rather than disinterest.

items.meaning: A polite and formal way to state that one already has a previous commitment.
items.example: Thank you for the invite, but I have a prior engagement.
items.plain: Thank you for the invite, but I already have plans.
items.note: A classic, diplomatic phrase for declining without revealing details.

items.meaning: Indicates that one is very busy or occupied with a specific task or commitment.
items.example: I'm rather tied up with a project deadline, unfortunately.
items.plain: I'm very busy with a project deadline, unfortunately.
items.note: A polite and slightly understated way to explain being unavailable due to work.

items.meaning: A polite and slightly hesitant way to indicate unavailability on a specific date.
items.example: I'm not quite free on the date you suggested, sadly.
items.plain: I'm not available on the date you suggested, unfortunately.
items.note: The 'quite' softens the refusal, making it sound less abrupt.

items.meaning: A polite way to decline an invitation or opportunity.
items.example: I'll have to pass on the invitation this time, thank you though.
items.plain: I won't be able to accept the invitation this time, thank you though.
items.note: A common and friendly way to decline, implying it's just for this occasion.

items.meaning: States that one cannot make a firm promise or decision about something.
items.example: I'm unable to commit to that date, as my schedule is uncertain.
items.plain: I can't promise to be available on that date, as my schedule is uncertain.
items.note: A clear and honest way to express uncertainty about future availability.

items.text: I'm not in a position to
items.form: I'm not in a position to
items.meaning: Explains that current circumstances prevent one from doing something.
items.example: I'm not in a position to host a dinner party right now.
items.plain: I can't host a dinner party right now due to my circumstances.
items.note: A polite and indirect way to decline, implying external factors are at play.

items.meaning: Politely explains that one's calendar is full or difficult to manage.
items.example: I'm afraid my schedule is rather packed for the foreseeable future.
items.plain: Unfortunately, my schedule is very full for the foreseeable future.
items.note: A diplomatic way to indicate limited availability without giving specific reasons.

items.meaning: A very formal and polite way to refuse an invitation or offer.
items.example: I must respectfully decline your kind invitation due to a prior commitment.
items.plain: I have to politely refuse your kind invitation due to a prior commitment.
items.note: Used in formal contexts, conveying utmost politeness and regret.

items.meaning: A common idiom meaning to feel slightly unwell or not at one's best.
items.example: I'm not feeling 100% today, so I'll have to take it easy.
items.plain: I'm not feeling completely well today, so I'll have to take it easy.
items.note: A casual and widely understood way to indicate mild illness or fatigue.

items.meaning: A polite way to say one is feeling unwell or not in top form.
items.example: I'm not feeling my best, so I think I'll stay home tonight.
items.plain: I'm not feeling very well, so I think I'll stay home tonight.
items.note: A gentle and common way to explain why one might decline social plans.

items.text: I'm not feeling up to par
items.form: I'm not feeling up to par
items.meaning: Indicates that one is not feeling as well or energetic as usual.
items.example: I'm not feeling up to par, so I'll have to miss the gathering.
items.plain: I'm not feeling as well as usual, so I'll have to miss the gathering.
items.note: A slightly more formal way to express feeling unwell, implying a standard of health.

items.text: I'm not feeling well enough to
items.form: I'm not feeling well enough to
items.meaning: Explains that one's health prevents participation in an activity.
items.example: I'm not feeling well enough to be good company tonight.
items.plain: I'm too unwell to be good company tonight.
items.note: A polite and specific way to decline, focusing on the impact of illness.

items.meaning: A polite and slightly formal way to express regret for unavailability.
items.example: My apologies, I'm not available on that particular evening.
items.plain: I'm sorry, I'm not free on that particular evening.
items.note: A courteous way to decline, often used in more formal or professional contexts.

items.meaning: An inviting phrase used by a host to encourage a guest to relax.
items.example: Please, make yourself comfortable while I get the drinks.
items.plain: Please, relax while I get the drinks.
items.note: A standard and warm welcoming phrase for guests.

items.text: Is there anything I can get you
items.form: Is there anything I can get you
items.meaning: A polite offer from a host to provide a guest with something they need.
items.example: Is there anything I can get you to make your stay more pleasant?
items.plain: Do you need anything to make your stay more pleasant?
items.note: A thoughtful and attentive way for a host to ensure guest comfort.

items.meaning: An invitation from a host for guests to serve themselves food or drink.
items.example: Help yourself to the snacks on the table, there's plenty.
items.plain: Please take some snacks from the table, there's plenty.
items.note: A common and friendly way to encourage guests to feel at home.

items.meaning: An informal request to someone to visit or contact you again soon.
items.example: It was lovely having you, don't be a stranger!
items.plain: It was lovely having you, please visit again soon!
items.note: A warm and friendly closing remark, encouraging future contact.

items.text: It was a real pleasure having you
items.form: It was a real pleasure having you
items.meaning: A sincere expression of enjoyment from a host after a guest's visit.
items.example: It was a real pleasure having you over for dinner last night.
items.plain: I truly enjoyed having you over for dinner last night.
items.note: A warm and genuine way for a host to thank a guest for their company.

items.meaning: A standard and polite expression of gratitude from a guest to a host.
items.example: Thank you for having me, I had a wonderful time.
items.plain: I appreciate you inviting me, I had a wonderful time.
items.note: The most common and essential phrase for a guest to use when leaving.

items.meaning: A common and sincere expression of enjoyment from a guest.
items.example: I had a lovely time at your party, everything was perfect.
items.plain: I really enjoyed myself at your party, everything was perfect.
items.note: A standard and warm way for a guest to express appreciation.

items.meaning: A polite and appreciative way to describe an enjoyable social event.
items.example: It was a delightful evening, thank you so much for hosting.
items.plain: It was a very pleasant evening, thank you so much for hosting.
items.note: A slightly more formal or elegant way to express enjoyment than 'lovely'.

items.meaning: Expresses sincere gratitude for someone's actions or hospitality.
items.example: I really appreciate you inviting me to your beautiful home.
items.plain: I'm very grateful that you invited me to your beautiful home.
items.note: A warm and heartfelt way to thank someone for their kindness.

items.meaning: A polite and appreciative response to a compliment, gift, or act of generosity.
items.example: Oh, you're too kind for bringing such a thoughtful gift!
items.plain: Oh, that's very generous of you for bringing such a thoughtful gift!
items.note: A common, slightly self-deprecating way to accept a compliment or gift graciously.

items.meaning: Offers to provide something or help financially for a shared event.
items.example: I'd be happy to contribute a dessert to the potluck.
items.plain: I would gladly bring a dessert to the potluck.
items.note: A polite and proactive offer to share the burden or cost of an event.

items.text: Let me know if I can
items.form: Let me know if I can
items.meaning: A polite offer to help or assist in any way needed.
items.example: Let me know if I can help with anything in the kitchen.
items.plain: Tell me if I can help with anything in the kitchen.
items.note: A common and helpful phrase for a guest to offer assistance to a host.

items.text: I'd be happy to lend a hand
items.form: I'd be happy to lend a hand
items.meaning: Offers to help with a task or chore.
items.example: I'd be happy to lend a hand with the tidying up.
items.plain: I would gladly help with the tidying up.
items.note: A friendly and proactive offer of practical assistance.

items.meaning: A warm and appreciative way to describe a very enjoyable social event.
items.example: It was a wonderful evening, thank you again for everything.
items.plain: It was a fantastic evening, thank you again for everything.
items.note: A sincere and positive closing remark after a pleasant social gathering.

items.text: I'm so glad you could make it
items.form: I'm so glad you could make it
items.meaning: Expresses genuine pleasure that someone was able to attend an event.
items.example: I'm so glad you could make it, we haven't seen you in ages!
items.plain: I'm very happy you were able to come, we haven't seen you in ages!
items.note: A warm and welcoming phrase from a host to a guest, especially if they haven't met in a while.

items.meaning: An informal expression meaning a very long time has passed since last contact.
items.example: It's been ages since we last saw each other, how have you been?
items.plain: It's been a very long time since we last saw each other, how have you been?
items.note: A common and friendly way to acknowledge a long gap in seeing someone.

items.text: We must do this again soon
items.form: We must do this again soon
items.meaning: Expresses a strong desire to repeat a pleasant social activity in the near future.
items.example: This was great, we must do this again soon.
items.plain: This was great, let's meet up again soon.
items.note: A common and warm closing remark after an enjoyable social interaction.

items.meaning: A friendly suggestion to maintain communication in the future.
items.example: Let's stay in touch and not let so much time pass.
items.plain: Let's keep communicating and not let so much time pass.
items.note: A common and warm way to end a conversation, encouraging future contact.

items.meaning: Expresses pleasure at renewing a relationship or friendship after a period apart.
items.example: It was great to reconnect with you after all these years.
items.plain: It was wonderful to get back in touch with you after all these years.
items.note: A sincere and appreciative way to acknowledge renewing an old acquaintance.

items.text: I'm keen to hear all about
items.form: I'm keen to hear all about
items.meaning: Expresses a strong and eager interest in learning details about something.
items.example: I'm keen to hear all about your new job and how it's going.
items.plain: I really want to hear all about your new job and how it's going.
items.note: A friendly and enthusiastic way to invite someone to share their news.

items.meaning: Indicates a plan or idea that is being considered, often for a social event.
items.example: I'm thinking of inviting a few people over for drinks next Friday.
items.plain: I might invite a few people over for drinks next Friday.
items.note: A casual way to float an idea for a social gathering without a firm commitment.

items.meaning: Expresses a desire or expectation for a future event or action.
items.example: I'm hoping to see you at the party on Saturday.
items.plain: I hope to see you at the party on Saturday.
items.note: A friendly way to express anticipation for someone's presence.

items.meaning: States an intention or arrangement for a future activity.
items.example: I'm planning on having a few friends over for dinner next week.
items.plain: I intend to have a few friends over for dinner next week.
items.note: A straightforward way to communicate upcoming social plans.

items.meaning: Indicates that one is thinking about a particular course of action or plan.
items.example: I'm considering hosting a potluck dinner next month.
items.plain: I'm thinking about hosting a potluck dinner next month.
items.note: A slightly more formal way to express an idea that is still in the planning stage.

items.meaning: Expresses a desire for a shared activity or outcome.
items.example: I'm hoping we can finally get together next week.
items.plain: I hope we can finally meet up next week.
items.note: A gentle way to suggest making plans, often after previous failed attempts.

items.meaning: Expresses a strong desire or enthusiasm for something.
items.example: I'm keen for a proper catch-up soon.
items.plain: I really want a proper catch-up soon.
items.note: Common in British English, indicating strong interest or desire.

items.meaning: Expresses willingness or enthusiasm to participate in an activity.
items.example: I'm up for anything, just let me know the details.
items.plain: I'm willing to do anything, just let me know the details.
items.note: A casual and enthusiastic way to agree to a suggestion.

items.meaning: Expresses enthusiastic willingness to participate in an activity.
items.example: I'm game for a hike this weekend if the weather holds.
items.plain: I'm willing to go for a hike this weekend if the weather holds.
items.note: A casual and eager way to agree to a plan, often implying adventure.

items.meaning: Expresses strong support or agreement for an idea or plan.
items.example: I'm all for trying that new restaurant you mentioned.
items.plain: I completely support trying that new restaurant you mentioned.
items.note: A strong and enthusiastic way to show approval.

items.meaning: Expresses a moderate to strong interest in something.
items.example: I'm quite keen on seeing that new exhibition.
items.plain: I'm quite interested in seeing that new exhibition.
items.note: A polite and genuine way to express interest, common in British English.

items.meaning: Expresses a polite but strong desire to do something.
items.example: I'm rather keen to hear about your new project.
items.plain: I'm quite eager to hear about your new project.
items.note: A slightly more formal or understated way to express strong interest.

items.meaning: Expresses a strong and genuine desire to do something.
items.example: I'm really keen to hear about your trip.
items.plain: I really want to hear about your trip.
items.note: A common and enthusiastic way to show interest, especially in British English.

items.meaning: Expresses extreme happiness or excitement about an opportunity.
items.example: I'm thrilled to be able to join you for the celebration.
items.plain: I'm extremely happy to be able to join you for the celebration.
items.note: A strong and genuine expression of joy, often for a special occasion.

items.meaning: Expresses great pleasure or happiness about something.
items.example: I'm delighted to accept your invitation to the party.
items.plain: I'm very happy to accept your invitation to the party.
items.note: A polite and warm way to express pleasure, often when accepting an invitation.

items.meaning: Expresses a feeling of privilege or special recognition.
items.example: I'm honoured to be invited to such a special event.
items.plain: I feel privileged to be invited to such a special event.
items.note: Used for significant or exclusive invitations, conveying deep appreciation.

items.meaning: Expresses satisfaction or happiness about something.
items.example: I'm pleased to confirm my attendance at your gathering.
items.plain: I'm happy to confirm my attendance at your gathering.
items.note: A polite and slightly formal way to express satisfaction or confirm something.

items.meaning: A polite way to state that one will attend an event.
items.example: I'm happy to confirm that I'll be there on Saturday.
items.plain: I'm pleased to say that I'll be there on Saturday.
items.note: A straightforward and friendly way to confirm attendance.

items.meaning: A strong assurance that one will attend an event.
items.example: I'll definitely be there, can't wait to see everyone.
items.plain: I will absolutely be there, can't wait to see everyone.
items.note: A common and confident way to confirm attendance.

items.meaning: A polite and friendly way to confirm attendance at an event.
items.example: I'll be sure to come along, thanks for the invite.
items.plain: I will definitely come, thanks for the invite.
items.note: Conveys a positive and reliable intention to join.

items.meaning: Promises to try very hard to achieve something, often to attend an event.
items.example: I'll make every effort to be there on time.
items.plain: I will try my hardest to be there on time.
items.note: Conveys strong intention, but acknowledges potential difficulties.

items.meaning: Promises to try hard to achieve something, often to attend an event.
items.example: I'll do my best to join you for the evening.
items.plain: I will try hard to join you for the evening.
items.note: A common and polite way to express intention, but with a hint of uncertainty.

items.meaning: Promises to make a strong effort, often implying potential difficulty.
items.example: I'll try my best to make it, but I have a prior engagement.
items.plain: I will try very hard to come, but I have a prior engagement.
items.note: A polite way to express willingness while also hinting at a possible conflict.

items.text: I'll see what I can do
items.form: I'll see what I can do
items.meaning: Indicates willingness to try and help or accommodate, but without a firm promise.
items.example: I'll see what I can do about shifting my schedule.
items.plain: I will try to shift my schedule.
items.note: A common, polite, and slightly non-committal response, implying effort will be made.

items.meaning: States that one needs to verify information before making a decision.
items.example: I'll have to check my calendar before I can commit.
items.plain: I need to look at my calendar before I can commit.
items.note: A standard and polite way to defer a decision until one can confirm availability.

i'm pleased to confirm.note: Checker slip: The expression is a standard formal phrase used to confirm attendance.

i'll be sure to come.note: Checker slip: The key accurately describes the phrase as a polite confirmation of attendance.
